records.our_prose: The mandarin (Citrus reticulata and its hybrids, including satsuma, clementine, and tangerine) is a subtropical evergreen fruit tree grown for small, sweet, loose-skinned, easy-to-peel fruit that is usually seedless. Its defining advantage over other sweet citrus is cold hardiness: satsuma is the most cold-tolerant of the commonly grown citrus, with mature trees withstanding brief lows near 15 to 20°F, notably colder than a navel orange, which lets in-ground mandarins reach zone 8 across the Gulf South and interior valleys. Early ripening (satsuma from fall) also gets the crop off the tree before the hardest winter cold. Mandarins need less summer heat than a navel to sweeten but want cool fall nights to color and drop acid, so they are marginal only in the cool-night tropics and the coolest coasts. Two group traits shape their care: seedless types set seeds if cross-pollinated by other citrus, so isolation preserves seedlessness; and mandarins are strongly alternate-bearing, managed by thinning heavy crops. Unlike a navel, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree and are picked promptly. Trees are small and grafted, usually on trifoliate-orange rootstock for cold hardiness, and productive for decades.

records.our_prose: Yellow mottling on the upper leaf surface with a matching blister-like swelling underneath that collapses into a brown-to-black, greasy-looking spot. Infected leaves drop, mostly in winter and early spring, thinning the canopy. It is a warm, humid-climate disease, most troublesome in Florida and the Gulf where relative humidity is high.

records.our_prose: Unlike a navel orange, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree. Satsuma and other early types puff (the rind separating and ballooning away from the flesh) and dry out if left on the branch past maturity, losing juice and flavor. The rind can look fine while the interior declines. This is the mandarin storage reality: pick promptly and refrigerate rather than storing on the tree.

records.our_prose: Harvest by taste and pick promptly. Mandarins color and sweeten with cool nights, but unlike a navel most types do not hold well on the tree: satsuma and early mandarins puff, dry, and lose flavor if left too long, so pick at maturity and refrigerate. The exceptions are the late holding types (Gold Nugget, Pixie), which do keep on the branch into spring. Early satsuma ripening also gets the crop off before the coldest winter nights.

records.our_prose: Harvest mandarins by taste, and pick promptly. The rind loosens and puffs slightly and color deepens as cool fall nights arrive, but in warm, humid climates the rind can stay green-tinged on fully ripe fruit, so taste rather than color decides. Unlike a navel, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree: satsuma and early types puff, dry, and lose flavor if left past maturity, so pick at ripeness and refrigerate. The exceptions are the late holding types, notably Gold Nugget and Pixie, which keep their quality on the tree into spring. Early satsuma ripening also lets the crop come off before the hardest winter cold.

records.our_prose: Valley winters rarely reach freezing. Satsuma-type mandarin, the hardiest common citrus, can withstand cold into the high teens°F once fully dormant, but an early cold snap before full dormancy, near 24°F, can still cause damage; that 18 to 24°F satsuma figure is genuinely from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension. Even so, this is the most cold-tolerant citrus in the Valley lineup. The winter-low band used here, roughly 26 to 32°F, is a synthesis anchored to the closest analog frost-free citrus regions, the milder Gulf Coast and the Arizona low desert, and the satsuma cold-damage datum, not a single figure Texas A&M AgriLife Extension publishes for the Valley.

records.our_prose: Plant a grafted nursery tree from a reputable source with certified disease-free stock. In cold-edge regions choose one on a trifoliate-orange rootstock for maximum cold tolerance. Container-grown trees can be planted year-round in frost-free zones; in cold-winter areas plant in spring after hard-freeze danger passes. Set the tree at the same soil line as in the nursery container, high on a mound, and never bury the graft union.

records.our_prose: The defining storage difference from a navel is that a mandarin does not hold well on the tree. Satsuma and most early mandarins should be picked promptly at maturity; left on the branch too long the fruit puffs, dries, and loses flavor. Refrigeration is the real storage method. The exceptions are the late holding types, notably Gold Nugget and Pixie, which do keep their quality on the tree for weeks into spring. Handle the thin-skinned fruit gently.
